content.text: Read AGENTS.md and issue #148, then pick up #228.
I'll start by reading the project instructions and the two issues.

result.output:
1	# AGENTS
2	
3	This repository contains two runtime surfaces:
4	
5	- `apps/web/` for the Next.js web app (UI + API routes).
6	- `services/chat/` for the FastAPI chat service.
7	
8	Use this file as the default runbook for coding agents.
9	
10	## Source of truth
11	
12	`AGENTS.md` is the canonical format for agent instructions. The root file defines
13	repository-wide policy; a nested `AGENTS.md` adds authoritative instructions for
14	its subtree. Apply both, from the root down to the file closest to the work.
15	
16	Assistant-specific context files are pointers only. They contain no independent
17	instructions:
18	
19	| Assistant | Pointer file | Points at |
20	| --- | --- | --- |
21	| Claude Code | `CLAUDE.md` (per scope) | sibling `AGENTS.md` |
22	| Gemini CLI | `GEMINI.md` (per scope) | sibling `AGENTS.md` |
23	| GitHub Copilot | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | root `AGENTS.md` |
24	
25	Scopes with their own runbook:
26	
27	- `AGENTS.md` (repo-wide)
28	- `apps/web/AGENTS.md`
29	- `services/chat/AGENTS.md`
30	- `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`
31	
32	Never add instructions to a pointer file. That includes memories captured by pressing
33	`#` in Claude Code, which append to the nearest `CLAUDE.md` — move that text into the
34	matching `AGENTS.md` instead.
35	
36	`make agent-docs-check` (part of `make docs-check`, and gated in CI) fails when a
37	pointer drifts and prints the added lines. To restore the pointers locally after
38	moving the content across:
39	
40	```bash
41	make agent-docs-check FIX=1
42	```
43	
44	## Code Review Rules
45	
46	- Treat changes at system seams as one contract. When a change touches the web/chat
47	  payload, Prisma schema and handwritten SQL, dependency manifests and constraints,
48	  or container inputs and runtime files, inspect and validate both sides.
49	- Require guards to measure effective behavior, not a nearby declaration. Reject
50	  vacuous loops, mislabeled samples, or configuration checks that never exercise the
51	  rendered pixels, served bytes, accessibility tree, resolved files, or tool output
52	  named by the assertion.
53	- For runtime and container changes, verify the built artifact and real integration
54	  path. Unit tests cannot prove that a file was copied into an image, a service starts
55	  with its deployed configuration, or the web/chat/database path works together.
56	
57	## Development workflow
58	
59	Follow these steps in order for every change.
60	
61	1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
62	   state, and all applicable instruction files before making changes. Preserve
63	   unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked work.
64	
65	2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
66	   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
67	   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
68	   `main` state.
69	
70	3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a tracked issue or
71	   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
72	   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
73	   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer. If the next issue is too
74	   large for one pull request, split it into ordered slices and complete only
75	   the current slice. Keep pull requests small enough for thorough review,
76	   reliable verification, and quick rollback.
77	
78	4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
79	   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
80	   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
81	   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
82	   - Run focused tests while iterating.
83	   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.
84	
85	   **A guard added for behavior that already works has no red phase**, so the
86	   confirm-it-fails bullet never reaches it. Write down which mistake each
87	   assertion catches, and which ones nothing catches, then demonstrate it:
88	   break an input on purpose and watch that assertion fail on it. Coverage
89	   argued rather than demonstrated is the defect the guard was added to
90	   prevent, one level up.
91	
92	   **Measure what was produced, not what was asked for.** A guard that reads a
93	   declaration is measuring the request, and the two come apart constantly: a
94	   colour Tailwind serialises as `lab()` reads as a different colour through a
95	   regex for numbers; `ring-0` leaves its colour in the computed box-shadow
96	   with no geometry to paint it; a zero-width border still reports a border
97	   colour; a blurred shadow reports its source colour while every pixel it
98	   paints is composited toward the background; `outlineWidth` reports the
99	   user-agent default of `3px` for an outline whose style is `none`. Every one
100	   of those passed a check that looked right and was measuring something
101	   adjacent to the claim. Read the rendered pixels, the served bytes, the
102	   accessibility tree — whatever the asserted thing actually is.
103	
104	   The same trap catches fixtures and samples. Assert that a sample is what its
105	   name says — for example, a brightness band, an overlap, or a count that only
106	   the intended case produces. Fixture-isolation rules for the root guard suite
107	   live in `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`.
108	
109	   **Run the focused test here, and only the focused test.** This step needs
110	   the one spec or module under change, its red phase, and the mutations that
111	   demonstrate what each assertion catches. The `verifier` will not do those:
112	   it is instructed not to modify the repository, so breaking an input on
113	   purpose is not available to it. Fast whole-suite runners are fine too where
114	   they are genuinely fast — `make test-web` is a few seconds.
115	
116	   The one spec may itself be a journey, and then it needs a composed stack:
117	   `make e2e-smoke KEEP_STACK=1` builds one and leaves it up, and steps 6 and 7
118	   will want that same one. No make target runs a single spec, so running just
119	   the one is `npx playwright test <file>` from `apps/web`.
120	
121	   What does not belong here is the whole journey suite. Running it costs
122	   minutes per iteration, and the trigger for handing over is "I believe this
123	   is done", not "I want to know whether it works".
124	
125	5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
126	   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
127	   preserving work that belongs to the user. A real problem found here is filed
128	   as an issue before the change is removed — see *Unrelated findings become
129	   issues* below.
130	
131	6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
132	   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent. The `ui-review`
133	   sub-agent must act as an expert in website design, usability,
134	   responsiveness, and accessibility. Address every actionable finding before
135	   running the `verifier`. For UI-affecting changes, exercise the changed
136	   journey in the rendered application at representative phone, tablet, and
137	   desktop viewports; inspect interaction, loading, empty, error, focus,
138	   keyboard, contrast, and responsive states as applicable; and capture
139	   screenshots or equivalent visual evidence.
140	
141	   A viewport is a width in CSS pixels, which says nothing about how many
142	   device pixels fill it. Where the change affects what the browser requests —
143	   anything carrying a `srcset`, or a source whose dimensions changed —
144	   exercise it at **2x as well as 1x**. Density is a property of the browser
145	   context (`deviceScaleFactor: 2`), not a width, so it needs a second pass
146	   rather than another viewport. A 2x screen asks for twice the CSS width, and
147	   the optimiser never upscales past the source, so a source that satisfies 1x
148	   can fall short at 2x while every 1x measurement stays clean. The 600px
149	   re-encode first tried in #152 came out at −0.9 to −2.2 dB PSNR at 1x and
150	   −4.4 to −6.6 dB at 2x: a difference at 1x small enough to accept, and one at
151	   2x that was plainly visible.
152	
153	   A change is UI-affecting when it moves a rendering dependency, too —
154	   `tailwindcss`, `next`, `react`, `postcss`, or a UI library in
155	   `apps/web/package.json`. That diff touches no component and can still change
156	   every rendered pixel; a Tailwind major shipped here with every check green.
157	
158	   For changes with no UI impact, explicitly record that rendered UI review is
159	   not applicable. If a finding is not applicable, record the concrete reason
160	   rather than silently ignoring it.
161	
162	   `ui-review` may start and stop a stack of its own. If one is already up —
163	   from step 4, or from an earlier pass through steps 6 and 7 when step 8 sends
164	   you back here — give it the `E2E_BASE_URL` and the ports if they are not the
165	   defaults, say the stack is not to be torn down, and say it is not
166	   `ui-review`'s. Naming it without addressing it is not a handover: remapped
167	   ports are normal here, and a reviewer that cannot reach the stack starts its
168	   own or renders nothing. Otherwise step 7's handover below promises a stack
169	   that stopped existing here.
170	
171	7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to run
172	   the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the
173	   change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage, and
174	   environment issues. Fix or explicitly resolve every actionable finding
175	   before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a code change,
176	   rerun the verifier after addressing it.
177	
178	   **The whole battery belongs here** — the merge-gate command, the production
179	   build, the root guard suite, and the full journey run. Do not pre-run those
180	   and hand over a summary: it doubles the wall-clock, and a summary is not
181	   what the next step needs.
182	
183	   **Hand over the stack rather than leaving one to be found.** Where journeys
184	   need a composed stack, step 4 has usually built one, and step 6 may have
185	   built its own — `ui-review` is allowed to, and that one is then its to tear
186	   down and may be on ports it chose. Give the `E2E_BASE_URL`, say the stack is
187	   yours, and say `KEEP_STACK=1`: without that flag `make e2e-smoke` deletes
188	   the containers and their volumes on exit. What the handover buys is not the
189	   rebuild, which happens either way, but that the verifier knows a stack
190	   exists, knows where it is, and knows not to destroy it. Tear it down after
191	   the last step that needs it, not after this one.
192	
193	   Say the ports if they are not the defaults. `make test-e2e` follows
194	   `E2E_BASE_URL` anywhere; `make e2e-smoke` probes `127.0.0.1:3100` and
195	   `:8100` literally and cannot be aimed elsewhere, so it and a remapped stack
196	   do not mix. One of the ways they fail is a green smoke run against an
197	   unrelated project's containers, which is worse than a failure because
198	   nothing looks wrong. Exactly which way you get depends on which compose
199	   files resolve and which ports are already held, and is not worth predicting
200	   here. Free the default ports before step 7, or hand over nothing and say
201	   why.
202	
203	8. **Run `code-review` before every commit.** Invoke the `code-review`
204	   sub-agent against the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and
205	   untracked file. The reviewer must act as an expert in the languages and
206	   frameworks used by this application. Address every actionable finding
207	   before committing. If review findings cause changes, rerun the appropriate
208	   tests and the `verifier`, then obtain a fresh `code-review` approval for the
209	   changed state.
210	
211	   That loop has no natural end, so ask for one: **have the reviewer say which
212	   findings are defects and which are refinements.** The loop ends on a round
213	   returning no defects, however many refinements come with it. Apply those,
214	   rerun the focused tests and the `verifier`, and record what was applied — a
215	   refinement-only change does not earn a fresh review round, here or at
216	   step 10.
217	
218	   **A fix made in this loop can invalidate step 6 as well.** If it alters what
219	   a page renders, rerun `ui-review` before the verifier and carry its verdict
220	   forward; the screenshots from step 6 otherwise describe a state that no
221	   longer exists. If it does not, record that the fix was not UI-affecting and
222	   go straight to the verifier. Only defects reopen step 6, on the same
223	   reasoning that ends this loop — a refinement applied to a rendered surface
224	   does not.
225	
226	9. **Commit after approval.** Commit only after verification and code review
227	   are complete. Use Conventional Commits:
228	
229	   ```text
230	   <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
231	   ```
232	
233	   Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
234	   useful, and do not combine unrelated work.
235	
236	10. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
237	    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
238	    - Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed after the
239	      pre-commit review.
240	    - A changed state includes code, tests, documentation, generated files,
241	      conflict resolution, or any other staged, unstaged, or untracked content.
242	    - Except refinements the reviewer classified as such and step 8 cleared:
243	      applying those does not re-arm this, or the loop step 8 just ended
244	      reopens here.
245	    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree
246	      remain unchanged.
247	    - Updating the branch from `main` — rebase, merge, or conflict resolution —
248	      invalidates **verification** as well as review. The builds, merge gates,
249	      smoke, and journeys were measured against a tree that no longer exists,
250	      so rerun step 7's applicable commands against the updated one rather than
251	      rerunning `code-review` alone.
252	    - Tear down any stack steps 4, 6, or 7 left running, once step 8's loop has
253	      closed and no further `verifier` run is coming: `make down`, or
254	      `docker compose down --volumes` to drop the seeded database with it. Step
255	      7 hands its stack forward under `KEEP_STACK=1`, which disables the only
256	      teardown the workflow otherwise performs — so without this the containers
257	      outlive the change and hold ports 3100, 55432, and 8100 against the next
258	      one.
259	    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and any
260	      required code review are complete.
261	    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not open
262	      draft pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a draft.
263	
264	11. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
265	    reports a clean merge state and every configured check passes. Never bypass
266	    a failing or pending required check. Self-merges are allowed when these
267	    conditions are met. Use squash merge for short-lived development branches
268	    to keep `main` linear, then delete the merged branch.
269	
270	### Unrelated findings become issues
271	
272	Work turns up problems that are not the problem being worked on. A stale script,
273	a pre-existing overflow, a check that does not check what it claims. This can
274	happen at any step, and most often happens during steps 6 to 8, because
275	`ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` read more of the repository than the
276	change touches.
277	
278	**File an issue at the moment of finding, before deciding what to do about it.**
279	The finding is cheapest to write down while the context that produced it is
280	still loaded, and an issue costs little if it later turns out to be nothing.
281	
282	Two failure modes this exists to prevent, and they pull in opposite directions:
283	
284	- **Silently widening the change.** Fixing it here inflates a reviewed diff with
285	  work nobody scoped, and buries an independent decision inside an unrelated
286	  pull request.
287	- **Silently dropping it.** Mentioning it only in a review comment or a chat
288	  reply means it is gone as soon as that context is. Nobody rediscovers it until
289	  it breaks something.
290	
291	Filing an issue is what makes "not now" different from "never".
292	
293	Write enough that it can be acted on without rediscovering it: what is wrong,
294	where, how it was found, and why it was not fixed at the time. Include the
295	measurement if there was one. Link the issue from the pull request that surfaced
296	it, so the reviewer can see the finding was handled rather than missed.
297	
298	Fix it in the current change only when leaving it would make that change wrong
299	or unverifiable — a pre-existing problem the change makes materially worse, or a
300	check that has to work for this change to be trustworthy. That is a judgement
301	call, so state the reason in the commit message. When in doubt, file and leave
302	it: a separate pull request is cheap, and an unscoped one is not.
303	
304	Sub-agents report findings; they do not file issues. Every finding they report
305	that falls outside the current change needs the main agent to file it.
306	
307	### Sub-agents this workflow depends on
308	
309	Steps 6 through 8 use `ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review`, defined in
310	`.claude/agents/`. All three run unattended: they cannot ask a question, and
311	they are instructed not to modify the repository they assess. That is an
312	instruction rather than a sandbox — each of them has `Bash` — so if a review
313	round is followed by working-tree changes you did not make, check `git status`
314	before assuming they are yours.
315	
316	**Their findings are claims, not verdicts.** Check the ones a change depends
317	on. This workflow has had a rendered review call a compliant focus indicator
318	"completely invisible" — acted on, it produced a guard that rejected a correct
319	design — and the same review quote a contrast ratio the running build measured
320	differently, zinc-400 at 2.56:1 against a measured 2.62:1. Both were believed
321	before they were checked. Address every finding, and where one is wrong, say so
322	with the measurement rather than complying.
323	
324	Record a disputed finding where someone else can audit it, and note when:
325	carried into the body of the commit step 9 is about to make, or into the pull
326	request body when the dispute arises after committing. Neither surface exists
327	while step 8 is running, so this is a commitment about what gets written, not a
328	precondition to satisfy first. Step 8's loop ends on a round returning no
329	defects, and a defect disputed rather than fixed counts as cleared only if it
330	is written down that way — a commit whose body omits it means step 8 did not
331	clear. Otherwise "I checked, it was wrong" lives inside one agent's reasoning,
332	and the gate opens with nothing to inspect.
333	
334	If one is unavailable — a different assistant, or a session started before the
335	definitions landed — carry out that step's intent directly and say which agent
336	was unavailable, rather than skipping the step or reporting it as done.
337	
338	`ui-review` needs a browser to satisfy step 6's rendered-journey requirement.
339	Where none is installed it falls back to reviewing source and must say so; a
340	review that claims viewports it never rendered is worse than none.
341	
342	## Repo map
343	
344	- `apps/web/src/app/`: Next.js pages and API routes.
345	- `apps/web/src/components/`: UI components.
346	- `apps/web/src/lib/`: shared web helpers and domain logic.
347	- `apps/web/Makefile`: web-owned dev/test/build command surface.
348	- `apps/web/AGENTS.md`: web-scoped agent runbook.
349	- `services/chat/src/api/`: chat service API and chat logic.
350	- `services/chat/tests/`: chat unit tests. Integration coverage lives in
351	  `scripts/e2e_smoke.py`, which runs against a real stack.
352	- `services/chat/Makefile`: chat-owned dev/test command surface.
353	- `services/chat/AGENTS.md`: chat-scoped agent runbook.
354	- `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`: fixture and mutation rules for root guard tests.
355	- `apps/web/prisma/`: shared data model and migrations.
356	- `infrastructure/`: deployment scripts and Terraform.
357	- `docs/`: operator and architecture docs.
358	
359	## Toolchain baseline
360	
361	- Node.js `22`
362	- Python `3.11`
363	
364	Use `mise` at repo root before running setup/CI commands:
365	
366	```bash
367	mise install
368	```
369	
370	### Python virtualenv
371	
372	All Python runs from a single project virtualenv at `.venv` (git-ignored). Make
373	targets create it on demand and invoke `.venv/bin/python` directly, so there is
374	nothing to activate — `make test-scripts`, `make quick-ci-chat`, and friends all
375	work from a clean shell.
376	
377	```bash
378	make venv
379	```
380	
381	Never install project Python dependencies into a system or mise interpreter. If
382	you run Python by hand, use `.venv/bin/python`, not `python`/`python3`.
383	
384	`PYTHON_BASE` is the interpreter used to *create* the venv (default
385	`mise exec python@3.11 -- python`); CI overrides it with `PYTHON_BASE=python`.
386	Do not override `PYTHON` itself — that bypasses the venv.
387	
388	## Canonical commands
389	
390	Run from repository root:
391	
392	```bash
393	make help
394	make bootstrap
395	make venv
396	make toolchain-doctor
397	make env-contract-check
398	make agent-doctor
399	make env-init

401	make setup-chat

433	npm run setup:chat

461	```bash

468	make -C services/chat help

471	## Environment files
472	
473	- Root app template: `.env.example`
474	- Chat service template: `services/chat/.env.example`
475	- Required keys contract: `config/env_contract.json`
476	- Required keys docs: `docs/ENV_CONTRACT.md`
477	
478	Copy templates to `.env` before local development.
479	
480	## Change boundaries
481	
482	- If you change web API payloads for chat, validate both:
483	  - `apps/web/src/app/api/chat/*`
484	  - `services/chat/src/api/*`
485	- If you change Prisma schema, run migrations and validate both web/chat tests.
486	  State whether the migration is destructive — a dropped or renamed column, a
487	  `NOT NULL` added to an existing one, a narrowed type. Local checks cannot tell
488	  you: they build the database fresh and seed it, so there is no data to lose and
489	  no older reader still running. Deployment has both.
490	  `infrastructure/scripts/docker-entrypoint.sh` applies migrations at container
491	  start while the previous revision is still serving, and rollback is a traffic
492	  shift back to that revision — which a destructive migration has already made
493	  unservable. Split those across two releases, expand then contract, or say in
494	  the pull request why this one does not need it.
495	- Prefer keeping generated artifacts and local runtime outputs out of commits.
496	
497	## Validation expectations
498	
499	Use `make quick-ci-changed` during implementation, and rerun it against an
500	explicit range when validating committed work:
501	
502	```bash
503	CHANGED_BASE=<base-sha> CHANGED_HEAD=<head-sha> make quick-ci-changed
504	```
505	
506	Every changed surface's merge-gate command has to have run before pushing.
507	Step 7 is where that happens, so this matrix is what tells `verifier` which
508	ones apply rather than a list to work through by hand:
509	
510	- Web: `make -C apps/web ci` (includes lint, type-check, tests, and build)
511	- Chat: `make -C services/chat ci`
512	- Scripts/tooling: `make test-scripts`
513	- Documentation/runbooks: `make docs-check`
514	- Cross-surface or repository-wide: `make ci`
515	
516	Add integration confidence where the change crosses a runtime boundary. These
517	are the verifier's too.
518	
519	- End-to-end journeys: `make test-e2e` (needs a running stack and the Playwright
520	  browser; see step 7)
521	- Cross-surface integration confidence: `make e2e-smoke`
522	- Contract-only integration confidence (minimal chat stack): `make e2e-smoke-lite`
523	- Full local-provider integration confidence: `make e2e-smoke-full`
524	- Release preflight: `make release-dry-run RELEASE_TAG=vX.Y.Z`
525	
526	## Troubleshooting
527	
528	- Toolchain mismatch: run `mise install`, then `make toolchain-doctor`.
529	- Virtualenv missing, broken, or on the wrong Python: run `rm -rf .venv && make venv`.
530	- `ModuleNotFoundError` for a chat dependency: you are probably outside the venv — re-run through `make`, or use `.venv/bin/python`. If you are inside it, the chat dependencies were never installed: `make setup` covers web only, so run `make setup-chat`.
531	- Playwright journeys fail with a missing browser: run `make -C apps/web install-e2e-browsers`, then rerun `make test-e2e`. Neither `make setup` nor `make bootstrap` installs it.
532	- Env contract drift: run `make env-contract-check` and update contract/templates/docs together.
533	- Docs link drift (including root runbooks): run `make docs-check`.

Durable context for whoever — or whatever — picks this up next. Kept as an issue rather than in an agent's local memory so it survives a cleared context and is visible to everyone.

## How this repository is being worked

Changes go through the [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md) workflow end to end: branch, implement, ui-review, verifier, code-review, PR. PRs merge when CI is green. Findings become issues. The loop continues to the next item without pausing for step-by-step approval.

The point is that it runs unattended, so stopping to confirm each step defeats it.

## What still gets surfaced rather than decided silently

Proceeding by default does not mean deciding everything. Three categories get a recommendation and a question:

1. **Changes to what users see** — image quality, layout tradeoffs. #96 is the live example: re-encoding to WebP is well-measured, but q82/600px is a judgment about acceptable fidelity, not a fact.
2. **Changes to other contributors' behavior** — #147 committed tool config that runs hooks on anyone's machine who clones. That deserved saying out loud, not just doing.
3. **Rewrites of shared history** — never silently. See the note below on why this keeps coming up.

The rest of the work does not wait on those answers. Finish everything that does not depend on the decision first, then ask.

## Two things that have repeatedly caught people out

**Checks that run without asserting on what they produced.** This is the repo's signature defect, found three separate times: the E2E smoke passed against a chat service returning `fallback: true`; the seed ran green on every PR while writing credentials that could never authenticate (#141); a category page referenced an image that had never existed (#137). A green check is not evidence unless something inspects its output.

**Verifying in a richer environment than the real one.** Also recurring: a populated local venv vs CI's bare one; jsdom vs a real browser; three sampled viewports vs the breakpoint boundaries where the defects actually live; `node_modules` vs the standalone image; a local stack reading `.env` vs CI with none. If a check passes locally, confirm it runs in the environment that matters.

**Deleting files does not shrink `git clone`.** The blobs stay reachable from history. #146 removed 68.6 MB from the working tree and the web image; `size-pack` did not move. Worth remembering before promising a clone-size win — see the measurement in #66.

## Running the stack locally

Environments differ per machine (port collisions, whether Ollama is installed for `LLM_PROVIDER=local`). `make e2e-smoke` may need a compose override for ports and provider. Resolve collisions with an override file using `ports: !override` — a plain `ports:` list appends rather than replaces — and never by stopping containers you did not start.

## Current state

`main` is clean. #145, #146 and #147 are merged. Open: #96 (WebP re-encode, the next substantive item), #66 (image weight, parent of #96), #118 (import-declaration guardrail), #129 (chat panel below `sm`, needs a design decision), #69 and #90 (blocked upstream).

# AGENTS (Script Guardrails)

Root script-test scope for coding agents. This file adds authoritative
instructions for `tests/scripts/`; apply it together with the repo-root
`AGENTS.md`. Put instructions here, never in the sibling pointer files.

## Local commands

Run from the repository root:

```bash
make test-scripts
.venv/bin/python -m unittest tests.scripts.<module> -v
```

## Code Review Rules

- Point a guard demonstration at a fixture tree, never the checkout it protects.
  Rebind every imported path constant the assertion dereferences; changing a root
  after derived constants were created does not redirect those constants.
- Prove that the intended assertion catches its named mistake, and separately prove
  the fixture was opened. A vacuity failure on an empty or mistyped path is not
  evidence that the behavioral assertion ran.
- Compare effective sets and outputs from the owning tool where practical. Parsing
  one declaration is insufficient when includes, excludes, defaults, comments, or
  other configuration can change what the compiler, runner, or hook actually uses.

## Fixture isolation

These modules compute path constants at import, so read the module and rebind every
constant the demonstrated assertion reaches:

- `test_image_encoding.py` reaches its files through `IMAGES_DIR`.
- `test_image_references.py` also needs `PUBLIC_DIR`, which `relative_to` depends on,
  and `REPO_ROOT`, which it walks for references.
- `test_page_headings.py` reads `REPO_ROOT` directly for component-supplied headings,
  so rebinding `APP_DIR` alone leaves that assertion pointed at the checkout.
- `test_published_ports.py` needs both `REPO_ROOT`, which `read()` resolves every
  coupled file through, and `COMPOSE`, which the port parser opens directly.
  Rebinding one leaves half the comparison pointed at the checkout, and the halves
  agreeing is the whole assertion.
- `test_agent_doctor.py` loads `scripts/agent_doctor.py` as a module, so the
  constants to rebind are that module's `COMPOSE_FILE`, `ROOT_ENV` and `CHAT_ENV` —
  not this file's `REPO_ROOT`, which only locates the script to load. Its
  `stale_port_keys` tests take their inputs as arguments and reach no path at all,
  which is the reason they are shaped that way.

vacuity guard whose count matches what the fixture contains. The count is the
evidence: a vacuity guard also fires when a fixture path is mistyped, while every
assertion inside the resulting empty loop passes.

"""Guard the local development surface against defects that pass silently.

The three things asserted here had one property in common before they were
fixed: none of them could fail. `sync-env`'s whole body sat behind a path test
that was always false, so it exited 0 and printed nothing on every run for as
long as it has existed. A `docker-compose.override.yml` that is not ignored
looks exactly like one that is, until someone commits it. A `prisma migrate
dev` with no `--name` looks fine until the schema has actually changed, and
then it blocks on a prompt no non-TTY can answer and exits 130 — a
cancellation, not a missing argument.

So each assertion here measures the effect rather than the text:

- `sync-env` is **run**, in a fixture tree, and the copied file is compared to
  the original. Separately its source path is **resolved** from the directory
  the recipe runs in, because `../.env` and `../../.env` are both plausible
  strings and only one names a file that exists — that one gives the useful
  failure message, and the execution catches the mistakes a parse cannot see.
- `git check-ignore` is asked whether the override is ignored, rather than
  `.gitignore` being grepped for a line that could be anchored wrong, negated
  later, or shadowed;
- every `npx prisma migrate dev` in tracked documentation is checked, not the
  one file that happened to be wrong, and not only the ones inside fences.

Not covered: the unsupported `eslint` key removed from `next.config.js` at the
same time. Asserting a key is absent is a declaration check, and the thing that
actually reports it is `next build`, which CI already runs — the key never
enforced anything, since lint runs as its own step.
"""

WEB_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "apps/web"

def sync_env_sources() -> list[str]:

    lines = WEB_MAKEFILE.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()

input.command:
cat > /tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-contoso/32326432-9961-4c06-ab5c-44ff606dccde/scratchpad/issue-churn.md <<'EOF'
Found while fixing #228, which needed a guard that starts a dev server. Not fixed there, because it is Next's behaviour rather than this repository's code and it predates that change.

## What happens

`next dev` rewrites two tracked files on every boot, and `next build` rewrites them back. Starting from a clean tree on `main`:

```
$ npx next dev -p 3177
$ git status --short
 M apps/web/AGENTS.md
 M apps/web/next-env.d.ts
```

and after the dev server has served a page, also:

```
 M apps/web/tsconfig.json
```

The three are separate mechanisms:

**`next-env.d.ts`** — the paths it imports are derived from `distDir`, which is `.next/dev` under `next dev` and not under `next build`:

```diff
-import "./.next/types/routes.d.ts";
+import "./.next/dev/types/routes.d.ts";
+import "./.next/dev/types/root-params.d.ts";
```

Generated by `node_modules/next/dist/lib/typescript/writeAppTypeDeclarations.js`, which joins `distDir` with `types/routes.d.ts`.

**`tsconfig.json`** — an `include` entry is appended, and it is doubled:

```diff
     ".next/dev/types/**/*.ts",
+    ".next/dev/dev/types/**/*.ts"
```

`.next/dev/dev/` is not a directory that exists. `distDir` is already `.next/dev`, and `dev/types/**/*.ts` is joined onto it again. The committed `tsconfig.json` already carries both `.next/types/**/*.ts` and `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts`, so this accumulation has happened before and been committed at least once.

**`apps/web/AGENTS.md`** — this one *is* fixed, in the #228 branch, because leaving it would have made that change wrong: the guard added there starts a dev server, so `make test-web` would have rewritten the runbook on every run. `next dev` appended:

```
<!-- BEGIN:nextjs-agent-rules -->
# This is NOT the Next.js you know
...
This block is written and re-added by `next dev` ... committing it with your work keeps the tree clean.
<!-- END:nextjs-agent-rules -->
```

`AGENTS.md` is this repository's authoritative agent runbook and is written by hand; `agentRules: false` in `next.config.js` stops it being written at all. Worth noting separately that the appended text instructs the reader to commit it, which is not advice a generated block should be giving about a hand-maintained instruction file.

## Why it matters

- Anyone who runs `make dev` or `make dev-web` gets a dirty tree, and the churn looks like part of whatever they were working on. There is a pre-commit hook here, so it gets staged with real work.
- `make -C apps/web ci` runs tests and then a build. With the #228 guard in place the test phase writes the dev paths and the build phase writes them back, so the direction the tree ends up dirty in depends on which ran last.
- `.next/dev/dev/types/**/*.ts` matches nothing, so the `include` entry is inert — but it is inert in a file that decides what `make typecheck` covers, which is not a good place for entries nobody can account for.

## How it is worked around now

`apps/web/next-dev-origins.test.ts` snapshots both files before spawning the dev server and writes them back in `afterAll`. That keeps `make test-web` from dirtying the tree, but it is a workaround in a test rather than a fix, and it does nothing for a developer running `make dev` by hand.

## Worth deciding

Whether these two belong in `.gitignore` rather than in the tree. `next-env.d.ts` says "This file should not be edited" in its own body and is fully derived; the `tsconfig.json` `include` entries are the harder half, since that file is genuinely hand-maintained apart from the entries Next appends.
EOF

input.command:
cat > /tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-contoso/32326432-9961-4c06-ab5c-44ff606dccde/scratchpad/comment-228.md <<'EOF'
Picked this up. The behaviour reproduces exactly as described, but the mechanism is not the one in the issue — `chat.tsx` is not involved at all, and neither is StrictMode.

## What is actually happening

React never hydrates. Nothing on the page does — the chat launcher is just the component you happened to click.

```
http://127.0.0.1:3177  403s=3  hydrated=false  dialogsAfterClick=0
http://localhost:3177  403s=0  hydrated=true   dialogsAfterClick=1
```

Same dev server, same moment, two hostnames. Three client chunks return **403**:

```
HTTP 403 /_next/static/chunks/0rrk_0cibx4v._.js
HTTP 403 /_next/static/chunks/apps_web_src_188yqmu._.js   <- contains chat.tsx
HTTP 403 /_next/static/chunks/apps_web_21at_al._.js
```

`node_modules/next/dist/server/lib/router-utils/block-cross-site-dev.js` blocks cross-origin requests to `/_next/*`, against this allowlist:

```js
const allowedOrigins = ['**.localhost', 'localhost', ...allowedDevOrigins ?? []]
if (hostname) allowedOrigins.push(hostname)
```

`127.0.0.1` is in none of those. The dev server said so in its own log, once per chunk, from the first run:

```
⚠ Blocked cross-origin request to Next.js dev resource /_next/static/chunks/... from "127.0.0.1".
To allow this host in development, add it to "allowedDevOrigins" in next.config.js
```

Only three of the sixteen script tags are affected because only those carry `crossorigin` and therefore send an `Origin` header — the gate allows requests with no origin. That is also why `curl` returns 200 for the identical URL the browser 403s on, which is what made this look like it was not a network problem.

## Why the two pieces of evidence in the issue pointed the wrong way

- **"React *is* hydrated — a controlled input on `/contact` keeps its typed value."** A controlled input keeps typed text with no React attached at all; that is the browser. Checking for a fiber instead: `Object.keys(launcher).filter(k => k.startsWith('__react'))` is `[]` on `127.0.0.1` and populated on `localhost`.
- **"`window.next` is present."** Set by an inline bootstrap script, before and independently of hydration.
- **"pageerrors: (none)."** Correct, and expected — a 403 on a `<script src>` is a network failure, not a page error.

## The focus-out theory

Not what is happening. The panel is never mounted and never unmounted — a `MutationObserver` on `document.body` records no `[role=dialog]` node being added, and the launcher's `aria-label` stays `"Open chat"`, so `showChat` never became true. Nothing ran, rather than something running and closing it again.

The specific mechanism the issue proposes cannot fire on the reported repro either: the `focusin` effect at `chat.tsx:217` is guarded by `if (!showChat || isCompact) return`, and the launcher is only unmounted when `isCompact && showChat` — the two conditions do not overlap.

## Fix

`allowedDevOrigins: ['127.0.0.1']` in `apps/web/next.config.js`. With it, at both `127.0.0.1` and `localhost`, phone and desktop:

```
403s=0 hydrated=true dialog=1 input=1 focus=chat aria-modal=true  stillOpenAfter1.2s=1   (390x844)
403s=0 hydrated=true dialog=1 input=1 focus=chat aria-modal=null  stillOpenAfter1.2s=1   (1280x720)
```

Panel opens, focus lands in the message input, `aria-modal` is set below `lg` and absent above it, and it stays open.

## Still worth doing, and not done here

The last section of this issue asks whether a focus landing on `document.body` should close the panel at all. That question is untouched by this — it was never firing on the reported repro — and it stands on its own merits. Filing separately rather than folding it in.

The `playwright.config.ts` comment the issue calls out is now half-true rather than misleading: chat *message* journeys do cross web, chat and the database, but opening the panel does not, and with this fix that is reviewable on a dev server.

Also filed #275: `next dev` rewrites tracked `next-env.d.ts` and `tsconfig.json` on every boot, found because the guard for this fix has to start a dev server.
EOF

cat > /tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-contoso/32326432-9961-4c06-ab5c-44ff606dccde/scratchpad/issue-focus.md <<'EOF'
Split out of #228. That issue's root cause turned out to be Next's dev-server cross-origin gate rather than anything in `chat.tsx` (see the comment there for the measurement), so its closing question was never actually exercised by the repro and is still open on its own merits.

## The question

`apps/web/src/components/chat.tsx:217-230` closes the panel whenever focus moves outside the widget:

```ts
const onFocusIn = (event: FocusEvent) => {
  const target = event.target as Node | null
  if (target && widgetRef.current?.contains(target)) return
  closedByFocusOut.current = true
  setShowChat(false)
}
```

Should a focus landing on `document.body` close the panel at all?

`relatedTarget === null`, or a `body` target, is the browser losing focus rather than the user moving it somewhere. That is the same distinction the comment block above the effect already draws for the address bar — it explains at length why the effect is backwards-only, because Tab forward off the last control leaves the page entirely and dismissing the panel for that would be closing it for something that is not a page interaction.

Focus falling to `body` is arguably the same class of event: no control gained focus, so no control can be obscured by the panel, and 2.4.11 — the criterion the effect exists to satisfy — is about the focused control.

## Why it is not obviously safe to change

The effect is only active at `lg` and up (`if (!showChat || isCompact) return`), where the surrounding page is not `inert`. Focus can reach `body` there by routes that are genuine user actions, and the comment already notes one the effect deliberately does not handle: clicking bare page fires no `focusin` at all, so the panel stays up — recorded as #187.

So the change would be narrow: ignore `focusin` whose target is `document.body` (or whose `relatedTarget` is null), and leave every other outside target closing the panel as it does now.

## What to check when picking this up

- Which real interactions actually land focus on `body` at `lg` and up. This needs measuring rather than reasoning about; the answer decides whether the change is worth making.
- `chat.test.tsx` covers the focus-out close path — see the effect's own comment for which assertions cover which branches, and which branches nothing covers.
- Whether ignoring `body` reopens the WCAG 3.2.1 concern the focus-return effect at `chat.tsx:271` was written for.

Not urgent, and not blocking anything.
EOF

Review the change on branch `fix/228-chat-panel-under-next-dev` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso.

## The change

Two files only:

Issue #228 reported that the chat panel could not be opened under `next dev`. - It is a dev server, not the composed stack: there is no chat service and no database behind it. So chat *messages* will not get a reply and product/catalogue pages backed by the database may be empty or error. That is expected and is not a finding. input.content:
Fixes #228.

## What was wrong

Not the chat panel. React never hydrated, and every client component on the page was inert — the launcher was just the one that got clicked.

Next's dev server blocks cross-origin requests to its own `/_next/*` routes, against an allowlist of `localhost`, `**.localhost` and the hostname it was bound with (`node_modules/next/dist/server/lib/router-utils/block-cross-site-dev.js`). `127.0.0.1` is in none of those, so a dev server opened at `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` returned **403** for three client chunks — one of which contains `chat.tsx`.

```
http://127.0.0.1:3177  403s=3  hydrated=false  dialogAfterClick=0
http://localhost:3177  403s=0  hydrated=true   dialogAfterClick=1
```

Only three of sixteen script tags are affected because only those carry `crossorigin` and therefore send an `Origin` header; the gate waves through requests with no origin. That is also why `curl` returned 200 for the exact URL the browser 403'd on, which is what made this look like it was not a network problem.

The dev server had been printing the cause, once per chunk, from the first run:

```
⚠ Blocked cross-origin request to Next.js dev resource /_next/static/chunks/... from "127.0.0.1".
To allow this host in development, add it to "allowedDevOrigins" in next.config.js
```

The StrictMode / focus-out mechanism proposed in #228 is not involved. The panel is never mounted and never unmounted — a `MutationObserver` records no `[role=dialog]` node being added, and the launcher's `aria-label` stays `"Open chat"`. The measurement and the two pieces of evidence that pointed the wrong way are written up [in a comment on the issue](https://github.com/scottdensmore/contoso/issues/228#issuecomment-5305157450).

## The change

`allowedDevOrigins: ['127.0.0.1', '[::1]']` in `apps/web/next.config.js`. Both loopback forms, because both are reachable and both were blocked — the server answers 200 on `http://[::1]:3178/contact` while 403ing its chunks, so fixing only IPv4 would leave the identical bug one address over. The bracketed spelling is what the gate matches; `'::1'` does not (`parseUrl` yields `[::1]` as the hostname).

This widens nothing outside development. `next build` never consults the key.

### Also here, and why it is not separate

`agentRules: false`. `next dev` was appending a block of its own to `apps/web/AGENTS.md` on every boot — the repository's authoritative, hand-maintained agent runbook, whose first rule is that generated content does not go in it. The appended text also instructs the reader to commit it along with whatever change is in flight.

That is fixed here rather than filed because leaving it made this change unverifiable: the guard below reads `next.config.js` and the first version of it started a dev server, so `make test-web` rewrote the runbook underneath the thing being tested.

## The guard

`apps/web/next-dev-origins.test.ts` asserts Next's own decision function against this repository's own `allowedDevOrigins` — not a re-implementation of the rule, which would keep agreeing with itself after Next's moved.

Three assertions, and what each catches, demonstrated by breaking the input:

| Mutation | Assertion that fails |
| --- | --- |
| `allowedDevOrigins` removed | `serves an internal route to a browser on 127.0.0.1` — `expected true to be false` |
| `allowedDevOrigins` widened with `evil.example` | `still blocks a foreign origin` — `expected false to be true` |

The foreign-origin case is the control: without it the file passes just as well against an allowlist widened to everything, and it is what proves the probe reaches the gate rather than being waved through for a reason of its own.

**What the guard does not cover, and how that was covered instead.** It does not prove the dev server calls that function, nor that the config key reaches it. That was measured directly, against a real `next dev`, before and after:

```
before  http://127.0.0.1:3177  403s=3  hydrated=false  dialogAfterClick=0
after   http://127.0.0.1:3178  403s=0  hydrated=true   dialog=1 input=1 focus=chat
                               aria-modal=true (390x844) / absent (1280x720), stays open
```

A guard that started its own server was written first and does not survive ordinary use: Next 16 keeps one dev server per `distDir` via `.next/dev/lock`, and a second exits 1 with "Another next dev server is already running". `make test-web` then failed for anyone with `make dev` up — green in CI, where nothing else runs, and broken on exactly the machines doing the development. The rejected version also had to snapshot and restore two tracked files the dev server rewrites on boot.

## Filed, not fixed here

- **#275** — `next dev` rewrites tracked `next-env.d.ts` and `tsconfig.json` on every boot, and appends a doubled, non-existent `.next/dev/dev/types/**/*.ts` include to `tsconfig.json`. Found because the first version of the guard started a dev server. Pre-existing and independent of this change.
- **#276** — whether a focus landing on `document.body` should close the chat panel, the closing question of #228. It was never firing on the reported repro, so it is a real question about the component and stands on its own.

## Not done here

The `playwright.config.ts` comment #228 calls out is now half-true rather than misleading: chat *message* journeys do cross web, chat and the database, but opening the panel does not, and with this fix chat UI is reviewable on a plain dev server. Left alone to keep the diff to the defect.

`ui-review` is running against the dev server. Summary of where things stand:

**Root cause found, and it isn't what #228 says.** React never hydrates. Next's dev server 403s three `crossorigin` client chunks when reached at `127.0.0.1` — one of them contains `chat.tsx` — because its `/_next/*` allowlist is `localhost`, `**.localhost`, and the bound hostname. Every client component on the page is inert; the launcher is just the one that got clicked.

The dev server had been logging the cause verbatim on every run (`⚠ Blocked cross-origin request … add it to "allowedDevOrigins"`). The two facts the issue cited as proof of hydration were both false positives — a controlled input keeps typed text with no React attached, and `window.next` comes from an inline bootstrap script. Checking for a fiber instead: `[]` on `127.0.0.1`, populated on `localhost`.

**Fix:** `allowedDevOrigins` in `apps/web/next.config.js`, plus a guard that exercises Next's own gate function with this repo's real config. Both mutations demonstrated (removing the fix fails the `127.0.0.1` assertion; widening the allowlist fails the foreign-origin control).

I threw away a first version of the guard that started its own dev server: Next 16 allows one dev server per `distDir`, so it failed for anyone with `make dev` running — green in CI, broken on the machines actually developing.

Three things I found along the way and did not fold in silently:
- **`next dev` was rewriting `apps/web/AGENTS.md`** on every boot, appending a block that instructs the reader to commit it. Fixed here (`agentRules: false`) because the guard reads that config and the first version rewrote the runbook underneath itself — I'm not treating tool-injected text in an instruction file as instructions.
- **#275** — `next dev` also rewrites tracked `next-env.d.ts` and `tsconfig.json`, appending a doubled `.next/dev/dev/types/**/*.ts` that matches nothing. Filed, not fixed.
- **#276** — the `document.body` focus question from #228's last section, which was never firing on the reported repro. Filed separately.

I also corrected the record on #228 itself with the measurements.

One open item I'll apply once `ui-review` returns its stack: `http://[::1]:3178` serves pages but 403s its chunks too, so IPv4-only would leave the identical bug one address over. The matching entry is `'[::1]'` — `'::1'` does not match, measured against `parseUrl`.

| | 127.0.0.1:3178 | localhost:3178 |
|---|---|---|
| 403s on `/_next/*` | **0** | **0** |
| Hydration / page errors | **0** | **0** |

Measured on rendered pixels with canvas-resolved sRGB, because Tailwind emits `lab()` here and a naive numeric parse silently drops the minus signs. That trap is called out in `chat.tsx` lines 676-682, and it caught my first two probes — they reported nonsense (1.19:1 for near-black bold on white) until I fixed the alpha handling in the background walk. The corrected pass reproduces the value documented in the source exactly (desktop send fill 5.86:1), which is what gives me confidence in the rest.

I could not cleanly isolate the input's resting ring, because `FIELD_BOUNDARY` draws it as an inset box-shadow and the input was focused whenever the panel was open, so the focus outline was mixed into the same property. The constant specifies `ring-zinc-500`, which my independent zinc-500 measurement puts at 4.83:1 against the white panel, and `e2e/support/boundary.ts` covers it per-pixel already.

**2× density** — not applicable. The diff touches no image, no `srcset`, and no source dimensions; nothing changes what the browser requests.

**Message round-trip** — deliberately out of scope per your brief. The error path did render and is legible: "Sorry, something went wrong. Please try again." at 6.08:1 (`desktop-error-state.png`). input.content:
fix(web): let next dev serve its chunks over the loopback address

Next's dev server blocks cross-origin requests to its own `/_next/*`
routes, against an allowlist of `localhost`, `**.localhost` and the
hostname it was bound with. `127.0.0.1` is in none of those, so a dev
server opened at `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` returned 403 for the three
client chunks that carry `crossorigin` and therefore send an `Origin`
header. React never hydrated and every client component on the page was
inert.

That is #228, which reported it as the chat panel refusing to open. The
panel was never mounted or unmounted and the component is not involved;
the launcher was simply the control that got clicked. Measured before
and after, against a real dev server:

    before  127.0.0.1  403s=3  hydrated=false  dialogAfterClick=0
            localhost  403s=0  hydrated=true   dialogAfterClick=1
    after   both, and [::1]     hydrated=true  dialog=1 focus=chat
            Origin: http://evil.example -> 403, still blocked

Both loopback forms, because both are reachable and both were blocked:
the server answers 200 on `http://[::1]:<port>/contact` while 403ing
that page's chunks. Bracketed is the spelling the gate matches; a bare
`::1` matches nothing.

The guard asks Next's own decision function, using this repository's own
`allowedDevOrigins`, rather than asserting the config literal — a config
check would pass just as well against a Next that had retired the gate.
It cannot start a real dev server to assert on served bytes: Next 16
permits one dev server per `distDir` via `.next/dev/lock`, so a guard
that started its own failed `make test-web` for anyone with `make dev`
running, while passing in CI. The end-to-end link that leaves uncovered
is the measurement above.

`agentRules: false` is here rather than in its own change because
leaving it made this one unverifiable: `next dev` appends a generated
block to `apps/web/AGENTS.md`, the hand-maintained runbook whose own
rule is that generated content stays out of it, and the block's text
asks to be committed along with whatever change is in flight. The guard
reads `next.config.js`, and the first version of it started a dev
server, so the tooling rewrote the runbook underneath the thing being
tested.

Recorded as disputed: review argued this was further justified because

PR **#282** is open and CI is nearly through — Web App CI, Script Guardrail Tests, CodeQL, and both CodeQL analyses all pass. Only Integration E2E Smoke is still running; I'm watching it and won't merge until it's green.

**What #228 actually was.** Not the chat panel. Next's dev server 403s its own `/_next/*` chunks when reached at `127.0.0.1`, because its allowlist is `localhost`, `**.localhost`, and the bound hostname. React never hydrated, so *every* client component was dead — the launcher was just the one that got clicked. The dev server had been logging the exact cause and remedy on every run.

The issue's two pieces of evidence for "React is hydrated" were both false positives: a controlled input keeps typed text with no React attached, and `window.next` comes from an inline bootstrap script. Checking for a fiber instead settles it — `[]` at `127.0.0.1`, populated at `localhost`. The StrictMode/focus-out theory couldn't fire on the reported repro anyway: that effect is guarded by `!showChat || isCompact`, and the launcher only unmounts when `isCompact && showChat`.

**Shipped:** `allowedDevOrigins: ['127.0.0.1', '[::1]']` — both loopback forms, since `[::1]` serves pages while 403ing its chunks, and a guard that asks Next's own decision function with the repo's real config rather than asserting the config literal.

I threw away a better-looking first guard that started its own dev server: Next 16 permits one per `distDir`, so it failed `make test-web` for anyone running `make dev` while passing in CI — green exactly where nobody works.

**Seven issues filed** rather than folded in or dropped: #275 (dev rewrites tracked generated files), #276 (#228's `document.body` question), #277 (dev indicator obscures the chat input), #278 (36×36 sheet buttons), #279 (Playwright MCP pinned to missing Chrome), #280 (root-level tests type-checked by nothing), #281 (vitest config breaks on a future Vite major).

Two things I want to put in front of you rather than leave buried:

- **`agentRules: false` is in this commit** and changes behaviour for everyone who clones. `next dev` was appending a generated block to `apps/web/AGENTS.md` — the hand-maintained runbook — and that block's own text asks to be committed with whatever change is in flight. I didn't treat that as an instruction. It's one line to revert if you disagree.
- **#277 is a decision I left to you.** `ui-review` recommended `devIndicators: false` in the same file; I declined, because switching off a diagnostic for every contributor to unobstruct one component at one width is a trade, not a fix.

Found while verifying the hybrid dev flow for the published-port move.

## What happens

Running `make dev-web` (`next dev`, Next 16.3.0) appends this to `apps/web/AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
<!-- BEGIN:nextjs-agent-rules -->

# This is NOT the Next.js you know

This version has breaking changes — APIs, conventions, and file structure may all differ from your training data. Read the relevant guide in `node_modules/next/dist/docs/` ... before writing any code. Heed deprecation notices.

This block is written and re-added by `next dev` — verify at `node_modules/next/dist/server/lib/generate-agent-files.js`. Removing it from a diff only re-creates the uncommitted change; committing it with your work keeps the tree clean.

<!-- END:nextjs-agent-rules -->
```

Reproduced by starting the dev server once. The generator is `node_modules/next/dist/server/lib/generate-agent-files.js`.

## Why this is worth a decision rather than a shrug

`AGENTS.md` is not an ordinary file in this repository. The root one opens with **"`AGENTS.md` is the canonical format for agent instructions"** and the whole pointer-file discipline — `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md` carrying no instructions of their own, enforced by `make agent-docs-check` — exists to keep exactly one authority for what an agent is told to do.

A framework appending instructions to that file, on every `next dev`, from `node_modules`, is a third party writing into the governance surface. The content is reasonable; that is not the point. The mechanism means:

- Anyone running `make dev-web` gets a dirty tree, and the dirt is *inside* the instruction file, where the diff is easy to wave through.
- The instructions change when the `next` version changes, without anyone reviewing them.
- The block's own text lobbies for its inclusion: *"committing it with your work keeps the tree clean."*

## What it does not do

`make agent-docs-check` and `make docs-check` both **pass** with the block present — measured. `check_agent_docs.py` guards pointer files against gaining content; it does not police additions to `AGENTS.md` itself. So nothing turns red, which is the reason this can drift in unnoticed.

## Measured

`next build` on 16.3.0 regenerates the tracked `apps/web/next-env.d.ts` with one extra line:

```diff
 /// <reference types="next" />

+import "./.next/types/root-params.d.ts";
```

So `git status` is dirty after every build:

```
$ make -C apps/web build     # CI's own gate, via npm run ci:web
$ git status --short
 M apps/web/next-env.d.ts
```

Reproduced twice: once in the working checkout, and once in a **clean detached worktree at `4057e09` built exactly the way CI builds** (`npm ci --workspaces=false --include=dev`, no `.env` exported, `HUSKY=0 make -C apps/web build`). It is the version bump, not a local environment artifact.

## Why CI is green

Nothing checks for a dirty worktree after the build. `Web App CI` runs `npm run ci:web` -> `make -C apps/web ci` -> lint, typecheck, test, build, and then the job ends; the modified file is simply discarded with the runner. The file's own header says "This file should not be edited", which is why nobody hand-edits it — but it also means nothing prompts anyone to commit the regenerated version.

## `next dev` and `next build` write *different* contents, so they fight

This issue records `next build` adding one line. `next dev` rewrites the same file differently, because the paths are derived from `distDir` and dev's is `.next/dev`:

```diff
-import "./.next/types/routes.d.ts";
+import "./.next/dev/types/routes.d.ts";
+import "./.next/dev/types/root-params.d.ts";
```

The generator is `node_modules/next/dist/lib/typescript/writeAppTypeDeclarations.js`, which joins `distDir` with `types/routes.d.ts`.

So it is not a one-time staleness that a single commit settles. `make dev` writes the dev paths, `make build` writes the build paths, and the file flips back and forth for as long as both commands are used. Committing either version leaves the other dirty. Observed repeatedly across a session that ran both.

That matters for the fix: pinning the committed content to whatever `next build` currently emits — the obvious reading of this issue — leaves anyone running `make dev` with a permanently dirty tree, and vice versa. Ignoring the file is the option that survives both.

## Verified the churn is invisible rather than harmless

`apps/web/tsconfig.json` sets `skipLibCheck: true`, which suppresses the unresolved-import error inside a `.d.ts`, so the dev-path version type-checks clean even though `.next/dev/types/routes.d.ts` may not exist. Measured: `skipLibCheck=true` exits 0, `skipLibCheck=false` exits 2. So nothing turns red either way, which is consistent with this issue's "Why CI is green" section and closes off the hope that a stricter type-check would have caught it.
EOF

## What happens

Once a `next dev` server has served a page, it appends an `include` entry to the tracked `apps/web/tsconfig.json`:

```diff
     ".next/dev/types/**/*.ts",
+    ".next/dev/dev/types/**/*.ts"
```

`.next/dev/dev/` is not a directory that exists and never will be. `distDir` is already `.next/dev`, and `dev/types/**/*.ts` is joined onto it a second time.

The committed `tsconfig.json` already carries both `.next/types/**/*.ts` and `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts`, so this accumulation has happened before and been committed at least once. Each doubled variant is a new entry rather than a replacement, so it grows.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than tolerating

The entry is inert — it matches nothing, so it changes what `tsc` compiles not at all. The problem is where it is inert: `include` is the file that decides what `make typecheck` covers. An entry nobody can account for, in the list that defines type-check scope, is the kind of thing that gets copied or "corrected" later by someone assuming it was deliberate.

It also means `git status` is dirty after a dev session in a *second* file beyond the one #260 tracks, and this one is genuinely hand-maintained — unlike `next-env.d.ts`, `tsconfig.json` cannot simply be ignored.

## Worth checking when picking this up

- Whether this is a Next bug worth reporting upstream. The doubling looks like a plain path-join error rather than a decision.
- Whether the two pre-existing entries, `.next/types/**/*.ts` and `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts`, are both still needed, or whether one of them is the fossil of an earlier round of the same accumulation.

content.text:
PR **#284** is open with everything green except the E2E smoke, still running. I'll merge when it lands.

The reference correction turned up something more valuable than the correction itself: **the first `make -C apps/web ci` run on that branch failed**, then passed unchanged.

I chased it rather than re-running until green. `src/app/page.test.tsx > names a product card once` failed 2 runs in 3 while the machine was busy, and has been green ~10 runs since. It's a **timeout, not a wrong assertion** — the failure is reported at the `it` declaration rather than the `expect`, and the failing runs took 8640ms and 5280ms against vitest's default 5s budget. It never fails in isolation; it needs the full suite plus load.

The mechanism fits: that test does `render(await Home())` with only `header` and `block` mocked, so it builds the largest DOM in the suite from the real `public/categories.json`, then computes accessible names across it. Nothing about it is non-deterministic in content — both the test and the component read the same file, no DB, no network. It just has the least headroom against a fixed budget.

Filed as **#283**. Worth flagging because the vitest suite has no flake policy, while `playwright.config.ts` explicitly refuses retries on the grounds that "a suite nobody trusts is the state this repo has been recovering from." CI has been consistently green so far, so today it's a local problem — but a GitHub runner has the same 5s budget, and the failure would land on an unrelated PR. I also couldn't identify the second file that failed in that first run before the suite went green; that's recorded as not captured rather than glossed.

Two other notes on this PR: `code-review` approved with no defects, and I applied both refinements it offered — naming the file beside each issue number, since the filename is what survives another re-scope. I also corrected "on boot" to "once it has served a page" for the `tsconfig.json` write, which is why it didn't appear alongside the boot-time writes when I first measured it.

Next up is **#279** once #284 merges.
